title: Introduction to Diabetes Mellitus and Classification

questions.q: Match the following criteria to the source's diagnostic pillars — 1) Fasting plasma glucose 2) 2-hour post-load 3) HbA1c … A) ≥126 mg/dL B) ≥200 mg/dL C) ≥6.5%
questions.exp: The three pillars are fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL, 2-hour post-load ≥200 mg/dL and HbA1c ≥6.5%; any one confirms diabetes in the absence of symptoms. (Book p917)

questions.q: An asymptomatic 50-year-old has fasting plasma glucose 132 mg/dL on two occasions. Which diagnostic label is most appropriate?
questions.exp: FPG ≥126 mg/dL confirmed on repeat testing confirms diabetes in an asymptomatic adult. (Book p917)

questions.q: Assess these diagnostic facts: I HbA1c ≥6.5% is diagnostic. II A single abnormal test is sufficient if symptomatic.
questions.exp: HbA1c ≥6.5% is one pillar of diagnosis; in symptomatic patients, a single random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms is diagnostic. (Book p917)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a value NOT diagnostic of diabetes?
questions.exp: HbA1c 5.9% is below the 6.5% threshold; HbA1c 7.0%, FPG 130 mg/dL and 2-h PG 220 mg/dL all meet diabetes criteria. (Book p917)

questions.q: The three pillars of diabetes diagnosis on this page are fasting glucose, 2-hour post-load and ___.
questions.exp: HbA1c is the third pillar; C-peptide, fructosamine and 1,5-AG are alternative markers but not part of the three-pillar definition. (Book p917)

questions.q: Match the following glucose state to its FPG / 2-h PG range — 1) Normal 2) Pre-diabetes / IGT 3) Diabetes … A) FPG <100, 2-h PG <140 B) FPG 100–125 or 2-h PG 140–199 C) FPG ≥126 or 2-h PG ≥200
questions.exp: Normal FPG is <100 mg/dL and 2-h PG <140 mg/dL; pre-diabetes (IFG / IGT) is FPG 100–125 or 2-h PG 140–199; diabetes is ≥126 or ≥200. (Book p917)

questions.q: A 45-year-old has FPG 118 mg/dL, 2-h PG 175 mg/dL and HbA1c 6.1%. The most consistent diagnostic label is:
questions.exp: Combined IFG (FPG 100–125) and IGT (2-h PG 140–199) with HbA1c 6.1% fits pre-diabetes. (Book p917)

questions.q: Assess diagnostic reproducibility: I A diagnosis requires confirmation on repeat testing in asymptomatic patients. II HbA1c can be falsely low in haemoglobinopathies.
questions.exp: Asymptomatic diagnosis is confirmed on repeat testing; HbA1c can be unreliable with haemoglobin variants, iron deficiency and pregnancy. (Book p917)

questions.q: Match the following state to its characteristic finding — 1) Normal 2) Pre-diabetes 3) Diabetes 4) Stress hyperglycaemia … A) HbA1c <5.7% B) HbA1c 5.7–6.4% C) HbA1c ≥6.5% D) Transient rise during acute illness
questions.exp: HbA1c <5.7% is normal; 5.7–6.4% is pre-diabetes; ≥6.5% is diabetes; transient stress hyperglycaemia resolves with illness. (Book p917)

questions.q: An asymptomatic patient has HbA1c 7.2% on one occasion. The next step is:
opts: Repeat the test on a different day to confirm
questions.exp: Without symptoms, the test should be repeated; if confirmed, lifestyle and metformin are typical first steps. (Book p917)

questions.q: Which value on this page is the diagnostic cut-off for HbA1c?
questions.exp: HbA1c ≥6.5% is the diagnostic cut-off; 5.7–6.4% defines pre-diabetes. (Book p917)

questions.q: An HbA1c of 5.7–6.4% on this page defines ___.
questions.exp: HbA1c 5.7–6.4% indicates increased risk for diabetes (pre-diabetes); 6.5% is the diagnostic cut-off. (Book p917)

questions.q: Assess additional tests: I Oral glucose tolerance test is more sensitive than FPG. IIGAD antibody screening is part of routine diagnosis.
questions.exp: OGTT is more sensitive than FPG for detecting IGT; GAD antibodies are used for classification after diagnosis, not routine diagnosis. (Book p917)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Match the following organ to its role in the ominous octet — 1) Liver 2) Pancreas (β-cell) 3) Skeletal muscle 4) Adipocyte … A) Increased gluconeogenesis B) Decreased insulin secretion C) Impaired GLUT4 translocation D) Increased lipolysis
questions.exp: The octet identifies liver (↑ gluconeogenesis), pancreas (↓ secretion), muscle (impaired GLUT4) and fat (↑ lipolysis) as four of the eight defects. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: A T2DM patient has fasting hyperglycaemia despite normal insulin sensitivity on clamp. Which octet member is most directly implicated?
opts: Increased hepatic gluconeogenesis (most important per source)
questions.exp: The page marks increased hepatic gluconeogenesis as the most important driver of fasting hyperglycaemia in T2DM. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Assess the octet: I β-cell dysfunction in T2DM is reversible with early therapy. II Skeletal muscle insulin resistance precedes β-cell failure.
questions.exp: β-cell dysfunction in T2DM is largely irreversible once established; muscle insulin resistance typically precedes β-cell exhaustion. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a tissue where insulin normally increases glucose uptake via GLUT4?
questions.exp: Liver uses GLUT2 (insulin-independent), whereas skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle and adipose tissue depend on insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Per the page, the single most important contributor to fasting hyperglycaemia in T2DM is increased ___.
questions.exp: Increased hepatic gluconeogenesis is the most important driver of fasting hyperglycaemia in T2DM on this page. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Match the following organ to its insulin-resistance effect — 1) Liver 2) Muscle 3) Adipocyte 4) Brain … A) ↑Gluconeogenesis B) ↓GLUT4-mediated uptake C) ↑Lipolysis / FFA flux D) Insulin-independent GLUT1 uptake
questions.exp: Insulin resistance in liver drives gluconeogenesis; in muscle impairs GLUT4; in adipose tissue increases lipolysis with FFA flux; brain glucose uptake is insulin-independent via GLUT1. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: An obese T2DM patient has high portal free-fatty-acid flux. The downstream effect on the liver is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Portal FFA flux drives hepatic gluconeogenesis and steatosis; it does not decrease VLDL output. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Assess this caveat: I CPT-1 is physiologically absent in liver; fatty-acyl-CoA accumulation in the schematic leads to insulin resistance. II Insulin normally suppresses hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes.
questions.exp: The schematic depicts CPT-1 as 'Absent in liver' which is biologically inaccurate; insulin normally suppresses HSL in adipocytes. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Match the following defect to the source's description — 1) β-cell 2) α-cell 3) Incretin axis 4) Kidney … A) Decreased insulin secretion B) Hyperglucagonaemia C) Reduced GLP-1 effect D) Increased glucose reabsorption (SGLT2)
questions.exp: β-cell defect is decreased insulin secretion; α-cell shows hyperglucagonaemia; incretin axis is reduced GLP-1 effect; the kidney shows increased SGLT2-mediated glucose reabsorption. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Which drug class targets the kidney component of the ominous octet?
questions.exp: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce renal glucose reabsorption; sulfonylureas target the β-cell; TZDs target adipose tissue; α-glucosidase inhibitors target intestinal carbohydrate absorption. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Which organ provides the dominant source of fasting endogenous glucose in T2DM?
questions.exp: Hepatic gluconeogenesis dominates fasting glucose production in T2DM. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: The 'ominous octet' highlights defects in pancreas, liver, muscle, fat, brain, gut (incretin), kidney and ___.
questions.exp: α-cell hyperglucagonaemia is the eighth member; the others include incretin deficiency, SGLT2 upregulation and CNS dysregulation. (Book p918)

questions.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
questions.q: Assess incretin physiology: I GLP-1 and GIP are secreted by intestinal cells. II The incretin effect is preserved in T2DM.
questions.exp: GLP-1 (L-cells) and GIP (K-cells) are secreted by the gut; the incretin effect is reduced in T2DM, prompting GLP-1 agonist therapy. (Book p918)

questions.q: Match the following classification to its example — 1) Type 1 2) Type 2 3) Gestational 4) Other specific types … A) Autoimmune β-cell destruction B) Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency C) Onset in pregnancy D) Monogenic, drug-induced, pancreatic disease
questions.exp: Type 1 is autoimmune β-cell destruction; Type 2 is insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency; GDM is diagnosed in pregnancy; 'other specific types' include monogenic, drug-induced and pancreatic diabetes. (Book p919)

questions.q: A 12-year-old presents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss and DKA. Anti-GAD is positive. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Children with DKA and positive GAD have autoimmune Type 1 diabetes, not Type 2 or MODY. (Book p919)

questions.q: Assess classification: I Type 2 diabetes is the most common form worldwide. II Latent autoimmune diabetes of adults (LADA) is a slow Type 1 variant.
questions.exp: Type 2 is the most common form; LADA is autoimmune diabetes in adults that is initially non-insulin requiring but slowly progresses. (Book p919)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a 'dirty dozen' cause of secondary diabetes?
questions.exp: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is associated with autoimmune diabetes (Type 1-like), not classical secondary 'dirty dozen' causes like pancreatitis, Cushing or steroids. (Book p919)

questions.q: Monogenic diabetes caused by HNF1A mutations and responsive to low-dose sulfonylureas is also known as ___.
questions.exp: MODY 3 (HNF1A) is the classic sulfonylurea-responsive monogenic diabetes; MODY 2 (GCK) is typically diet-controlled. (Book p919)

questions.q: Match the following MODY subtype to its key feature — 1) HNF1A-MODY (MODY 3) 2) GCK-MODY (MODY 2) 3) HNF4A-MODY (MODY 1) … A) Sulfonylurea-responsive, progressive B) Mild stable hyperglycaemia, often no Rx C) Macrosomia + neonatal hypoglycaemia then diabetes
questions.exp: HNF1A-MODY (MODY 3) is sulfonylurea-responsive and progressive; GCK-MODY (MODY 2) is mild and usually not treated; HNF4A-MODY is associated with macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia. (Book p919)

questions.q: A 24-year-old with mild fasting hyperglycaemia and a family history of 'mild diabetes' across three generations has HbA1c 6.0%. Genetic testing is most likely to find:
questions.exp: Mild stable hyperglycaemia across generations fits GCK-MODY (MODY 2); HNF1A-MODY is progressive and typically requires treatment. (Book p919)

questions.q: Assess autoimmune screening: I GAD, IA-2 and ZnT8 antibodies classify autoimmune diabetes. II Antibody-negative autoimmune diabetes is impossible.
questions.exp: GAD, IA-2 and ZnT8 are the principal autoantibodies; a small subset of autoimmune diabetes is antibody-negative (so-called idiopathic Type 1). (Book p919)

questions.q: Match the following test to its role — 1) Fasting glucose 2) 2-hour OGTT 3) HbA1c 4) C-peptide … A) Screening and diagnosis B) Sensitive for IGT C) Reflects chronic glycemia D) Endogenous insulin secretion
questions.exp: Fasting glucose is the workhorse screening test; OGTT is most sensitive for IGT; HbA1c reflects chronic glycemia; C-peptide reflects endogenous insulin secretion. (Book p919)

questions.q: A 50-year-old has fasting glucose 105 mg/dL but 2-hour post-load 168 mg/dL. The most consistent label is:
questions.exp: 2-hour glucose 140–199 with normal FPG is isolated IGT. (Book p919)

questions.q: The diagnostic 75-g OGTT detects ___ more sensitively than fasting glucose.
questions.exp: The 75-g OGTT detects IGT earlier than fasting glucose. (Book p919)

questions.q: Assess fructosamine and 1,5-AG: I They reflect shorter-term glycemia than HbA1c. II They are useful when HbA1c is unreliable.
questions.exp: Fructosamine and 1,5-AG reflect 2–3 weeks of glycemia, useful in pregnancy or haemoglobinopathies where HbA1c is unreliable. (Book p919)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a test that does NOT assess chronic glycaemia?
questions.exp: Random plasma glucose is a snapshot; HbA1c, fructosamine and 1,5-AG all integrate glycaemia over different windows. (Book p919)

questions.q: Match the following pre-diabetes interventions — 1) Lifestyle 2) Metformin 3) Bariatric surgery 4) Insulin sensitisers (TZDs) … A) 7% weight loss + 150 min/week activity B) Considered in high-risk patients <60 yr C) For BMI ≥35 with comorbidities D) Pioglitazone reduced progression
questions.exp: Lifestyle with 7% weight loss and 150 min/week activity is first-line; metformin is added in high-risk patients under 60; bariatric surgery is for BMI ≥35 with comorbidities; pioglitazone has RCT evidence for progression reduction. (Book p920)

questions.q: A 45-year-old BMI 32 has pre-diabetes with HbA1c 6.3%. Three months of lifestyle change produced no improvement. The most consistent next step is:
questions.exp: Metformin is added for high-risk pre-diabetes patients with persistent hyperglycaemia despite lifestyle change. (Book p920)

questions.q: Assess pre-diabetes screening: I BMI ≥25 (printed as 'overweight') plus another risk factor is the threshold. II Screening begins at age 25–60 (printed '2–60').
questions.exp: Screening is recommended for BMI ≥25 plus risk factors; ADA typically recommends starting at age 35, not 25–60 (note: the source's 'Age 2-60yrs' is an inconsistency that should be flagged as the typical ADA recommendation is ≥35). (Book p920)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out among metformin contraindications?
questions.exp: eGFR ≥45 is not a contraindication; the others are contraindications or cautions (eGFR <30 contraindication, hepatic failure and alcoholism caution). (Book p920)

questions.q: The page's metformin dose threshold for withholding in CKD is eGFR < ___ mL/min/1.73 m².
questions.exp: Metformin is contraindicated at eGFR <30; dose-reduced between 30–45. (Book p920)

questions.q: Match the following target to the population — 1) Most non-pregnant adults with diabetes 2) Older / frail with comorbidities 3) Pregnancy with pre-existing diabetes … A) HbA1c <7% B) HbA1c 7.5–8% or higher C) HbA1c <6–6.5% if achievable without hypoglycaemia
questions.exp: Most adults target HbA1c <7%; older frail patients tolerate 7.5–8%; pregnancy pre-existing diabetes aims for <6.5% if achievable safely. (Book p920)

questions.q: An 80-year-old nursing-home resident with multimorbidities has T2DM and frequent hypoglycaemia. The most appropriate HbA1c target is:
questions.exp: Elderly frail patients tolerate a relaxed target of 7.5–8% to avoid hypoglycaemia. (Book p920)

questions.q: Assess targets: I A1c-Derived Average Glucose (ADAG) provides an estimated mean glucose. II SMBG is not needed with HbA1c.
questions.exp: ADAG links HbA1c to mean glucose; SMBG remains essential, especially in insulin-treated patients. (Book p920)

questions.q: Match the following SMBG pattern to population — 1) Type 1 on basal-bolus 2) Type 2 on metformin only 3) Pregnancy with GDM on insulin 4) Stable Type 2 with HbA1c 6.8% … A) ≥4 checks/day B) Less frequent, fasting or paired C) Frequent daily checks D) Routine not required
questions.exp: Type 1 basal-bolus needs ≥4 checks/day; metformin-only T2DM benefits from fewer paired checks; GDM on insulin needs frequent checks; well-controlled T2DM may not need routine SMBG. (Book p920)

questions.q: A T1DM patient on basal-bolus has HbA1c 8.5% with frequent hypoglycaemia. The next step is:
opts: Stop SMBG and rely on HbA1c
Review SMBG data, adjust insulin and consider CGM
questions.exp: Frequent hypoglycaemia with elevated HbA1c prompts review of SMBG data, insulin adjustment and CGM to reduce variability. (Book p920)

questions.q: Pre-diabetes is sometimes treated with ___ in high-risk women with prior gestational diabetes.
questions.exp: Metformin is recommended in high-risk patients, including women with prior GDM. (Book p920)

questions.q: Assess pre-diabetes: I A1c 6.0% is normal. II HbA1c ≥6% with risk factors is an indication for intervention.
questions.exp: HbA1c 5.7–6.4% is pre-diabetes; ≥6% with risk factors is sufficient for intervention in many algorithms. (Book p920)

questions.q: Match the following diabetes subtype — 1) LADA 2) Type 3c (pancreatogenic) 3) Type 4 (gestational) 4) MODY … A) Slow autoimmune diabetes in adults B) Diabetes following pancreatic disease C) Diabetes diagnosed in pregnancy D) Monogenic autosomal dominant diabetes
questions.exp: LADA is slow autoimmune diabetes in adults; type 3c is pancreatogenic diabetes after pancreatic disease; type 4 is gestational diabetes; MODY is monogenic autosomal dominant diabetes. (Book p921)

questions.q: A 38-year-old non-obese patient with GAD positivity initially responds to metformin but progresses to insulin within 4 years. The most consistent label is:
questions.exp: Slow autoimmune diabetes in non-obese adults progressing to insulin fits LADA; MODY would be antibody negative and autosomal dominant. (Book p921)

questions.q: Assess LADA: I GAD, IA-2 and ZnT8 antibodies can be present. II Patients usually avoid insulin for years.
questions.exp: LADA shares the same antibody panel as Type 1 diabetes; patients often avoid insulin for months to a few years but progress. (Book p921)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a feature of LADA rather than Type 2 diabetes?
questions.exp: Obesity with central adiposity is characteristic of Type 2; LADA features persistent antibodies, non-obese phenotype and earlier insulin need. (Book p921)

questions.q: Type 3c diabetes (pancreatogenic) is most commonly due to chronic ___ in adults.
questions.exp: Chronic pancreatitis is the most common cause of pancreatogenic diabetes; cystic fibrosis, pancreatic cancer and haemochromatosis are other causes. (Book p921)

questions.q: Match the following diabetes subtype to its key clue — 1) MODY 2 (GCK) 2) MODY 3 (HNF1A) 3) Mitochondrial diabetes 4) Wolfram syndrome … A) Mild stable hyperglycaemia, low Rx need B) Progressive sulfonylurea-responsive C) Maternal inheritance with deafness D) Diabetes insipidus, optic atrophy, deafness
questions.exp: MODY 2 (GCK) is mild; MODY 3 (HNF1A) is sulfonylurea-responsive; mitochondrial diabetes shows maternal inheritance with deafness; Wolfram syndrome has DI, optic atrophy and deafness (DIDMOAD). (Book p921)

questions.q: A young patient with diabetes also has sensorineural deafness and a maternal family history. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Maternal inheritance with diabetes and deafness fits mitochondrial diabetes (MIDD, MELAS-related). (Book p921)

questions.q: Assess Wolfram syndrome: I It includes diabetes insipidus, optic atrophy and deafness. II It is also called DIDMOAD.
questions.exp: Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) is characterised by DI, optic atrophy, deafness and diabetes mellitus. (Book p921)

questions.q: Match the following subtype to its antibody / genetic marker — 1) LADA 2) MODY 3 3) Type 3c (pancreatogenic) 4) Mitochondrial … A) GAD antibody positive B) HNF1A mutation C) Anti-GAD negative, exocrine insufficiency D) mtDNA 3243A>G mutation
questions.exp: LADA is GAD-positive; MODY 3 has HNF1A mutation; pancreatogenic diabetes is GAD-negative with exocrine insufficiency; mitochondrial diabetes is associated with the 3243A>G mutation. (Book p921)

questions.q: A 45-year-old with chronic pancreatitis and new diabetes has low C-peptide and steatorrhoea. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Diabetes following chronic pancreatitis with low C-peptide and exocrine insufficiency fits type 3c pancreatogenic diabetes. (Book p921)

questions.q: Type 3c diabetes is associated with both endocrine and ___ insufficiency.
questions.exp: Type 3c combines endocrine and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, distinguishing it from Type 2 diabetes. (Book p921)

questions.q: Assess type 4 diabetes: I Gestational diabetes is diagnosed at 24–28 weeks. II Persisting after delivery is labelled GDM; resolving excludes future risk.
questions.exp: GDM is typically screened at 24–28 weeks; persistence postpartum defines overt diabetes, and even resolving GDM signals long-term risk. (Book p921)

questions.q: Match the following metabolic syndrome criterion to the cutoff (per source/standard) — 1) Waist circumference (men) 2) Triglycerides 3) HDL (men) 4) BP … A) ≥90 cm (Asian Indian) B) ≥150 mg/dL C) <40 mg/dL D) ≥130/85 mmHg
questions.exp: Asian-Indian waist circumference cut-off for men is ≥90 cm; triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL; HDL <40 mg/dL in men; BP ≥130/85 mmHg. (Book p922)

questions.q: A 50-year-old South Asian man has BP 132/86 mmHg, fasting TG 165 mg/dL, HDL 38 mg/dL and waist circumference 95 cm. The diagnostic label is:
questions.exp: Three of five criteria (waist, TG, HDL, BP) are met; this is metabolic syndrome. (Book p922)

questions.q: Assess BMI categories: I Asian-Indian overweight is BMI ≥23. II Obesity is BMI ≥25 in Asian-Indian classification.
questions.exp: Asian-Indian BMI thresholds: overweight ≥23, obesity ≥25 (compared with WHO ≥25 and ≥30). (Book p922)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out among metabolic syndrome criteria?
questions.exp: Fasting glucose is a metabolic syndrome criterion in NCEP-ATP III but not in IDF's primary central obesity definition; waist is central to IDF criteria. (Book p922)

questions.q: The page's Asian-Indian BMI cut-off for overweight is ___.
questions.exp: Asian-Indian cut-offs: normal <23, overweight ≥23, obese ≥25 (with morbid obesity at higher values). (Book p922)

questions.q: Match the following milestone in T2DM history — 1) First clinical use 2) Role of UKPDS 3) Discovery … A) 1921 insulin (later refined for type 2) B) Demonstrated benefit of glycaemic control C) Insulin by Banting and Best
questions.exp: Insulin was discovered in 1921; first clinical use came shortly after; UKPDS established benefit of glycaemic control in T2DM. (Book p922)

questions.q: A 50-year-old with BMI 26, BP 138/88, TG 178 mg/dL, HDL 36 mg/dL and FPG 102 mg/dL asks about diabetes risk. The most consistent label is:
questions.exp: Metabolic syndrome is present; FPG 100–125 places the patient in the pre-diabetes range. (Book p922)

questions.q: Assess waist cut-offs: I Asian-Indian women use a lower waist cut-off than men. II IDF uses the same Asian waist cut-off for men and women.
questions.exp: Asian women use ≥80 cm (vs ≥90 cm men); IDF uses the same Asian-specific cut-off for both sexes but is sex-specific. (Book p922)

questions.q: Match the following to its discovery timeline — 1) Insulin 2) Sulfonylureas 3) Metformin 4) GLP-1 agonist … A) 1921 B) 1940s–50s C) 1950s (biguanides) D) 2005 onwards
questions.exp: Insulin 1921; sulfonylureas mid-20th century; metformin (biguanides) widely adopted mid-century; GLP-1 agonists from 2005. (Book p922)

questions.q: An Asian-Indian patient with BMI 27 has BP 128/82, TG 145 mg/dL, HDL 42 mg/dL and FPG 92 mg/dL. The patient meets:
questions.exp: BMI 27 exceeds the Asian-Indian obesity cut-off ≥25 and waist typically ≥90 cm; BP, TG and HDL do not meet criteria. (Book p922)

questions.q: The metabolic syndrome criterion for fasting plasma glucose is ≥ ___ mg/dL.
questions.exp: Fasting plasma glucose ≥100 mg/dL (or treatment) is one of the metabolic syndrome criteria. (Book p922)

questions.q: Assess these facts: I South Asians have higher diabetes risk at lower BMIs. II Metabolic syndrome increases cardiovascular risk beyond its components.
questions.exp: South Asians have higher risk at lower BMIs (the basis of Asian-Indian cut-offs); metabolic syndrome increases CV risk beyond individual components. (Book p922)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: Match the following Type 1 autoantibody to its prevalence / target — 1) GAD65 2) IA-2 3) ZnT8 4) Anti-insulin … A) ~70–80% at diagnosis B) ~60–70% at diagnosis C) >95% in some populations D) More common in children
questions.exp: GAD65 is positive in roughly 70–80% at diagnosis; IA-2 in 60–70%; ZnT8 in over 95% in some populations; anti-insulin is more common in children. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: A 22-year-old non-obese patient has new diabetes, positive GAD and rapidly progresses to insulin. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Non-obese young adult with GAD positivity and rapid progression fits Type 1 diabetes. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: Assess these facts: I HLA-DRB1*04 increases Type 1 risk. IIGAD antibodies are also seen in stiff-person syndrome.
questions.exp: HLA-DRB1*04 is a susceptibility allele for Type 1 diabetes; GAD antibodies also occur in stiff-person syndrome and cerebellar ataxia. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: Which is the odd one out — an antibody NOT typically associated with Type 1 diabetes?
questions.exp: Anti-CCP is associated with rheumatoid arthritis, not Type 1 diabetes. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: ZnT8 antibodies target the zinc transporter in pancreatic ___ cells.
questions.exp: ZnT8 is expressed in pancreatic β-cells, making it a specific autoimmune target. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: Match the following test to its use in T1DM — 1) C-peptide 2) Autoantibody panel 3) HbA1c 4) Insulin level … A) Reflects endogenous insulin secretion B) Classifies autoimmune diabetes C) Monitors chronic glycaemia D) Affected by exogenous insulin and hepatic clearance
questions.exp: C-peptide measures endogenous insulin secretion; autoantibody panel classifies autoimmune diabetes; HbA1c monitors chronic glycaemia; insulin level is confounded by exogenous insulin and hepatic clearance. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: An 18-year-old with new T1DM has undetectable C-peptide and positive ZnT8. The most consistent interpretation is:
opts: Autoimmune β-cell destruction with no residual function
Type 2 diabetes with severe insulin resistance
questions.exp: Undetectable C-peptide with ZnT8 indicates autoimmune β-cell failure in Type 1 diabetes. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: Assess T1DM genetic risk: I HLA-DR3 and DR4 increase risk. II Most T1DM is monogenic.
questions.exp: HLA-DR3 and DR4 (DRB1*03 and *04) increase susceptibility; most T1DM is polygenic, not monogenic. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: Match the following antibody to the population where it's most useful — 1) Insulin autoantibody 2) GAD 2) ZnT8 3) IA-2 … A) Children <5 yr at onset B) Adults >30 yr at onset C) Combined with GAD for sensitivity D) Highly specific for T1DM
questions.exp: Insulin autoantibody is most useful in young children; GAD is more often positive in adult-onset T1DM/LADA; ZnT8 combined with GAD improves sensitivity; IA-2 is highly specific for T1DM. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: A 5-year-old with new diabetes has positive insulin autoantibodies but negative GAD and IA-2. The most consistent interpretation is:
questions.exp: Insulin autoantibodies are common in young children with T1DM; one antibody plus clinical phenotype is sufficient to support diagnosis. (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: Triple antibody positivity (GAD, IA-2, ZnT8) in a newly diagnosed adult is highly suggestive of ___ rather than Type 2.
questions.exp: Triple positivity in adults strongly suggests autoimmune diabetes (Type 1-like or LADA). (Book p923)

questions.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
questions.q: Assess C-peptide: I It is cleaved from proinsulin in equimolar amounts. II C-peptide is a surrogate for endogenous insulin.
questions.exp: C-peptide is cleaved from proinsulin in equimolar amounts with insulin and is used as a surrogate for endogenous insulin secretion. (Book p923)

questions.q: Match the following insulin-resistance syndrome — 1) Type A 2) Type B 3) HAIR-AN 4) Donohue / Rabson-Mendenhall … A) Defective insulin receptor gene B) Anti-insulin-receptor autoantibodies C) Hyperandrogenism, IR, acanthosis D) Severe insulin-receptor mutations with childhood mortality
questions.exp: Type A insulin-resistance is due to insulin-receptor gene mutations; Type B is autoimmune with anti-receptor antibodies; HAIR-AN combines hyperandrogenism, IR and acanthosis nigricans; Donohue / Rabson-Mendenhall are severe receptor-mutation syndromes with childhood mortality. (Book p924)

questions.q: A teenage girl has severe acanthosis nigricans, oligomenorrhoea and elevated testosterone with normal glucose initially but develops diabetes at 18. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance and acanthosis nigricans fit HAIR-AN. (Book p924)

questions.q: Assess insulin-resistance syndromes: I Type A is autoimmune in origin. II Donohue syndrome presents with intrauterine growth restriction.
questions.exp: Type A is genetic (receptor mutations), Type B is autoimmune; Donohue syndrome includes intrauterine growth restriction and severe neonatal features. (Book p924)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a MODY subtype?
questions.exp: Type A insulin-resistance is a receptor disorder, not a MODY subtype; the others are common MODY subtypes. (Book p924)

questions.q: Donohue and Rabson-Mendenhall syndromes are caused by mutations in the ___ gene.
questions.exp: Both are due to severe insulin-receptor mutations (INSR). (Book p924)

questions.q: Match the following MODY subtype to its genetic defect — 1) MODY 2 2) MODY 3 3) MODY 5 (HNF1B) … A) Glucokinase (GCK) B) HNF1A transcription factor C) HNF1B with renal cysts
questions.exp: MODY 2 is GCK; MODY 3 is HNF1A; MODY 5 is HNF1B with renal cysts and genital tract anomalies. (Book p924)

questions.q: A 22-year-old with mild hyperglycaemia, family history of mild diabetes, and renal cysts on ultrasound is most likely to have:
questions.exp: MODY 5 (HNF1B) is associated with renal cysts and genital tract malformations. (Book p924)

questions.q: Assess MODY: I MODY is typically autosomal dominant. II MODY 3 often progresses and requires sulfonylurea therapy.
questions.exp: MODY is autosomal dominant; HNF1A-MODY (MODY 3) is progressive and sulfonylurea-responsive. (Book p924)

questions.q: Match the following neonatal diabetes gene — 1) KCNJ11 2) ABCC8 3) INS … A) K-ATP channel, sulfonylurea-responsive B) K-ATP channel, sulfonylurea-responsive C) Insulin gene mutation
questions.exp: KCNJ11 and ABCC8 encode K-ATP channel subunits and are sulfonylurea-responsive; INS is the insulin gene mutation form. (Book p924)

questions.q: A 6-week-old with persistent hyperglycaemia is found to have a KCNJ11 mutation. The most appropriate therapy is:
questions.exp: KCNJ11 mutations causing neonatal diabetes are often successfully switched to high-dose sulfonylureas. (Book p924)

questions.q: Gestational diabetes mellitus is screened at ___ weeks of gestation.
questions.exp: Universal GDM screening is recommended at 24–28 weeks; high-risk women are screened earlier. (Book p924)

questions.q: Assess GDM: I It is associated with increased future Type 2 diabetes risk. II First-line pharmacotherapy is glyburide.
questions.exp: GDM raises future Type 2 diabetes risk; first-line pharmacotherapy is insulin, with metformin or glyburide as alternatives. (Book p924)

questions.q: Match the following pancreatic disease to its diabetes risk — 1) Chronic pancreatitis 2) Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma 3) Cystic fibrosis 4) Haemochromatosis … A) Most common cause of type 3c diabetes B) New-onset diabetes can be a presenting feature C) CFRD with insulin deficiency D) Iron deposition causing β-cell loss
questions.exp: Chronic pancreatitis is the most common cause of type 3c; pancreatic cancer can present with new-onset diabetes; cystic fibrosis causes CFRD; haemochromatosis deposits iron in β-cells. (Book p925)

questions.q: A 65-year-old with new-onset diabetes has weight loss and epigastric pain; CT shows a pancreatic mass. The most consistent interpretation is:
opts: New-onset diabetes as a presenting sign of pancreatic cancer
Type 2 diabetes with weight loss from low calorie diet
questions.exp: New-onset diabetes with weight loss and pancreatic mass raises suspicion for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. (Book p925)

questions.q: Assess type 3c: I Insulin therapy is usually required. II Metformin is the preferred first-line therapy in type 3c.
questions.exp: Type 3c diabetes usually requires insulin because of combined endocrine and exocrine deficiency; metformin is not first-line. (Book p925)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a drug that causes hyperglycaemia?
questions.exp: Metformin is hypoglycaemic; glucocorticoids, tacrolimus and olanzapine cause hyperglycaemia. (Book p925)

questions.q: New-onset diabetes after solid-organ transplantation is most commonly caused by ___ therapy.
questions.exp: Calcineurin inhibitors, especially tacrolimus, are common causes of post-transplant diabetes. (Book p925)

questions.q: Match the following antibody result to its subtype on the page's algorithm — 1) High antibodies 2) Low antibodies 3) No antibodies … A) T1DM B) LADA C) T2DM or MODY
questions.exp: The algorithm maps high antibodies to T1DM, low antibodies to LADA and no antibodies to T2DM or MODY. (Book p925)

questions.q: A 45-year-old non-obese patient has high GAD antibody titre and progresses to insulin within 2 years. The most consistent diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Slow autoimmune progression in non-obese adult fits LADA. (Book p925)

questions.q: Assess this caveat: I The page's algorithm labels 'Low antibodies' as T1DM and 'High antibodies' as LADA. II The C-peptide table on p928 reverses these patterns.
questions.exp: The page's arrow scheme appears inverted (high antibody → T1DM, low → LADA); the C-peptide table on p928 uses the standard pattern (T1DM low C-peptide, LADA intermediate). Note this inconsistency when teaching. (Book p925)

questions.q: Match the following drug to its diabetogenic mechanism — 1) Glucocorticoids 2) Olanzapine 3) Tacrolimus 4) Pentamidine … A) Increase gluconeogenesis and IR B) Weight gain and IR via H1 antagonism C) Direct β-cell toxicity D) β-cell destruction causing hypoglycaemia then diabetes
questions.exp: Steroids drive gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance; olanzapine causes weight gain and IR via histamine antagonism; tacrolimus has direct β-cell effects; pentamidine causes β-cell destruction with biphasic glycaemia. (Book p925)

questions.q: A patient with Cushing disease has worsening diabetes despite escalating metformin. The most appropriate next step is:
questions.exp: Treating the underlying hypercortisolism is essential; insulin is often needed regardless until cortisol is controlled. (Book p925)

questions.q: Pentamidine is associated with ___ glycaemia initially, then diabetes.
questions.exp: Pentamidine initially causes hypoglycaemia through β-cell destruction, followed by diabetes. (Book p925)

questions.q: Assess these diabetogenic drugs: I Protease inhibitors can cause insulin resistance. II Niacin causes hyperglycaemia.
questions.exp: Protease inhibitors (especially indinavir) cause insulin resistance; niacin also worsens glycaemia. (Book p925)

questions.q: Match the following diabetes association — 1) Haemochromatosis 2) Cushing 3) Acromegaly 4) Pheochromocytoma … A) Bronze diabetes from iron deposition B) Hypercortisolism-induced IR C) Excess GH-induced IR D) Catecholamine-induced hyperglycaemia
questions.exp: Haemochromatosis causes bronze diabetes from iron deposition; Cushing produces hypercortisolism-induced insulin resistance; acromegaly causes GH-induced IR; pheochromocytoma causes catecholamine-induced hyperglycaemia. (Book p926)

questions.q: A 50-year-old with hypertension, centripetal obesity and purple striae has new diabetes. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Centripetal obesity, hypertension and purple striae suggest Cushing syndrome as the secondary cause of diabetes. (Book p926)

questions.q: Assess acromegaly: I Diabetes improves with treatment of GH excess. II Diabetes persists despite cure of acromegaly in most patients.
questions.exp: Diabetes improves with control of GH excess in many acromegaly patients; in some, diabetes persists despite cure. (Book p926)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out — a non-pancreatic endocrine cause of diabetes?
questions.exp: Insulinoma is a pancreatic tumour that causes hypoglycaemia, not hyperglycaemia; the others cause hyperglycaemia. (Book p926)

questions.q: Bronze skin, hepatomegaly and new-onset diabetes suggest ___.
questions.exp: Bronze skin with hepatomegaly and diabetes fits hereditary haemochromatosis; iron studies confirm. (Book p926)

questions.q: Match the following diagnostic clue to the cause — 1) Elevated transferrin saturation 2) Elevated urinary free cortisol 3) Elevated IGF-1 4) Elevated plasma metanephrines … A) Haemochromatosis B) Cushing syndrome C) Acromegaly D) Pheochromocytoma
questions.exp: Transferrin saturation supports haemochromatosis; urinary free cortisol supports Cushing; IGF-1 supports acromegaly; plasma metanephrines support pheochromocytoma. (Book p926)

questions.q: A patient on protease inhibitors has new diabetes. The mechanism is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Protease inhibitors cause insulin resistance rather than autoimmune destruction. (Book p926)

questions.q: Assess post-transplant diabetes: I It is associated with worse graft outcomes. II Tacrolimus has a lower diabetogenic potential than ciclosporin.
questions.exp: Post-transplant diabetes worsens graft outcomes; tacrolimus is more diabetogenic than ciclosporin. (Book p926)

questions.q: Match the following endocrine tumour to its metabolic effect — 1) Glucagonoma 2) Somatostatinoma 3) VIPoma 4) Insulinoma … A) Necrolytic migratory erythema + diabetes B) Inhibits insulin secretion C) WDHA syndrome D) Hypoglycaemia
questions.exp: Glucagonoma causes necrolytic migratory erythema with diabetes; somatostatinoma inhibits insulin; VIPoma causes WDHA; insulinoma causes hypoglycaemia. (Book p926)

questions.q: A patient with weight loss, necrolytic migratory erythema and diabetes most likely has:
questions.exp: Necrolytic migratory erythema with diabetes is the textbook glucagonoma presentation. (Book p926)

questions.q: The classic triad of pancreatic cholera is watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and ___.
questions.exp: VIPoma causes WDHA: watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and achlorhydria. (Book p926)

questions.q: Assess these endocrine syndromes: I Acromegaly with diabetes is an indication for IGF-1 measurement. II Pheochromocytoma always presents with sustained hypertension.
questions.exp: Acromegaly diagnosis requires elevated IGF-1; pheochromocytoma typically presents with paroxysmal, not always sustained, hypertension. (Book p926)

units.title: Diabetes definition and three pillars
units.sec: Diabetes definition and three pillars · p917
units.guide: Anchor the three pillars (FPG ≥126, 2-h PG ≥200, HbA1c ≥6.5%) and pre-diabetes ranges. Asymptomatic diagnosis requires repeat testing; oral glucose tolerance test detects IGT earlier than fasting glucose.

units.title: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM
units.sec: Ominous octet and pathophysiology of T2DM · p918
units.guide: Map the eight defects: pancreas (β/α), liver (gluconeogenesis), muscle (GLUT4), fat (lipolysis), brain, gut (incretin), kidney (SGLT2). Note the schematic's 'CPT-1 absent in liver' is biologically inaccurate; insulin normally suppresses HSL in adipocytes.

units.title: Dirty dozen, classification, diagnostics
units.guide: Distinguish Type 1, Type 2, gestational and other specific types. MODY 3 (HNF1A) is sulfonylurea-responsive; MODY 2 (GCK) is mild and rarely treated; autoimmune screening uses GAD, IA-2 and ZnT8.

units.title: Pre-DM treatment, screening, HbA1c targets
units.sec: Pre-DM treatment, screening, HbA1c targets · p920
units.guide: Lifestyle (7% weight loss, 150 min/week) is first-line; metformin is added for high-risk patients; metformin is contraindicated at eGFR <30. Most adults aim HbA1c <7%, elderly 7.5–8%, pregnancy <6.5%.

units.title: Classification: LADA, type 3c, type 4, monogenic
units.sec: Classification: LADA, type 3c, type 4, monogenic · p921
units.guide: LADA is slow autoimmune diabetes in non-obese adults; Type 3c is pancreatogenic; GDM is pregnancy-onset. Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) and mitochondrial diabetes (MELAS-related) are rare monogenic forms.

units.title: Type 2 history, metabolic syndrome, BMI
units.sec: Type 2 history, metabolic syndrome, BMI · p922
units.guide: South Asians face higher diabetes risk at lower BMIs (overweight ≥23, obese ≥25). Metabolic syndrome combines waist, BP, TG, HDL and fasting glucose criteria; insulin, sulfonylureas, metformin and GLP-1 agonists each mark a discovery milestone.

units.title: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation
units.sec: T1DM markers, autoimmunity and antibody interpretation · p923
units.guide: GAD, IA-2 and ZnT8 are the principal autoantibodies; ZnT8 positivity exceeds 95% in some populations. C-peptide measures endogenous insulin; insulin level is confounded by exogenous insulin. HLA-DR3/DR4 increase T1DM risk.

units.title: Insulin-resistance syndromes, MODY, type 4
units.guide: Type A insulin-resistance is genetic (INSR), Type B is autoimmune. HAIR-AN combines hyperandrogenism, IR and acanthosis; Donohue and Rabson-Mendenhall are severe receptor mutations. KCNJ11 and ABCC8 mutations cause sulfonylurea-responsive neonatal diabetes.

units.title: Pancreatic and drug-induced diabetes algorithm
units.sec: Pancreatic and drug-induced diabetes algorithm · p925
units.guide: Chronic pancreatitis causes most type 3c diabetes; pancreatic cancer can present with new-onset diabetes. Glucocorticoids, tacrolimus, antipsychotics and pentamidine are notable diabetogenic drugs. Note the algorithm's arrow scheme appears inverted vs the C-peptide table on p928.

units.title: Diabetes associations and review
units.guide: Haemochromatosis causes 'bronze diabetes'; Cushing, acromegaly and pheochromocytoma are endocrine causes of secondary diabetes. Glucagonoma presents with necrolytic migratory erythema and diabetes; VIPoma causes WDHA.
